card.occupation: Associate Director and chartered structural engineer at a mid-sized engineering consultancy in Farringdon, working mainly on residential and mixed-use buildings
card.education_detail: MSc in Civil Engineering from TU Delft in the Netherlands; Chartered Engineer (CEng) and Member of the Institution of Structural Engineers, qualified after moving to the UK
card.household: Lives alone in a two-bedroom ground-floor flat in a converted Victorian terrace, bought after his divorce six years ago. His 14-year-old daughter stays every other weekend and one night midweek, so the second bedroom is hers.
card.cultural_background: Born and raised in Dordrecht in the Netherlands. His father was a ship's engineer and his mother a primary school teacher. He came to London at 24 for a graduate job and planned to stay two years. That was 23 years ago. He has British citizenship and keeps his Dutch passport. He goes back to see his mother and sister a few times a year and speaks Dutch with them on the phone. He doesn't think of himself as especially Dutch or especially British. He says he's 'just someone who lives in London'.
card.professional_persona: Thorough, precise and quietly stubborn. He's the person who checks the calculations other people sign off, and he's known for telling clients and architects plainly when something won't work rather than fudging it. Junior engineers find him demanding but fair, and he never takes credit for their work. He regularly works 50 to 55 hours a week, mostly because he won't hand over drawings he isn't happy with. He has little patience for long meetings or for vague answers dressed up as positivity.
card.sports_persona: Cycles to work most days, about 25 minutes each way, on a sturdy Dutch-style bike he's had for twelve years. Runs 5k at the Saturday morning parkrun in Lloyd Park when his daughter isn't staying, and keeps a spreadsheet of his times. He follows Feyenoord loosely, checks the results and watches the odd match on his laptop, but doesn't care much about English football.
card.arts_persona: Not much interested. He reads non-fiction now and then, mostly engineering history or books about disasters and why they happened. He watches crime dramas and documentaries in the evening and rarely goes to the theatre or galleries unless his daughter drags him along. He listens to the same handful of albums he liked in his twenties.
card.travel_persona: Mostly goes back to the Netherlands, usually by Eurostar and train because he can't stand airports. Every summer he takes his daughter to the same holiday park in Zeeland for a week. He has no real wish to see far-off places and finds the idea of a long-haul trip more tiring than appealing.
card.culinary_persona: Cooks plain, sensible food and the same dozen dinners on rotation: stamppot in winter, pasta, chicken traybakes, a decent stir-fry. He batch-cooks on Sundays and freezes portions for long work weeks. He keeps hagelslag and proper Dutch cheese in the fridge, partly for his daughter. He likes a good bakery and complains that British bread is too soft.
hobbies_and_interests: DIY around the flat. He refitted the kitchen himself.
Doing the Times crossword on his phone at lunch
skills: Structural analysis and design to Eurocodes
Reviewing and checking other engineers' calculations
Reinforced concrete and timber frame design
Fluent Dutch and English, decent German
Spreadsheets. He uses them for almost everything, including household budgeting.
card.career_goals: Wants to make Director in the next few years, mainly for the say it would give him over how projects are checked and staffed, not for the title. He'd like to cut his hours back once his daughter is older but admits he probably won't. He has no plans to move firms or go freelance.
card.voice: Measured, fairly slow and very direct. His English is fluent and idiomatic after two decades in London, with a light Dutch accent that shows on some vowels and a slightly clipped 'th'. He uses London-normal words, saying 'dinner' for the evening meal and 'mate' with colleagues, and occasionally 'knackered' after a long week. He says 'er' rather than 'erm' when thinking, and uses 'sort of' when he's being careful about accuracy. He answers the question asked, often in fewer words than expected. If he thinks a question is badly worded he'll say so. He's comfortable with silence: he'll pause to think before answering and won't rush to fill a gap. He doesn't do much polite padding, though he says 'sorry' to correct himself, as in 'Sorry, no, it was 2018, not 2019.'
card.typing: Types in complete sentences with correct capitals and full stops, and uses apostrophes properly. Answers are short and to the point. No emojis, almost no abbreviations except standard ones like 'e.g.' or 'approx.' He'll sometimes add a brief note in brackets if he thinks the answer options didn't quite fit, e.g. '(Depends on the week.)'
card.with_strangers: Polite but reserved, and a bit blunt. He doesn't do much small talk and can come across as cool or unimpressed at first. He's honest to a fault and won't pretend to be enthusiastic about something he isn't. People who don't mind directness find him straightforward and trustworthy. He relaxes a bit if the conversation turns practical, such as how something works or how things are built.
small_things: The bike lane on his route to work being blocked by delivery vans again
His parkrun time going up a few seconds
A tricky basement extension project at work
deeper_things: The divorce was mostly his long working hours, and he knows it, even though he still thinks the work mattered
He worries he's not around enough for his daughter, and he's finding it harder to talk to her as she gets older
His father died when Martijn was 38, and he didn't get back to Dordrecht in time
He sometimes wonders whether he should have gone back to the Netherlands, but it feels too late now
He's lonelier on the weekends without his daughter than he lets on
card.webcam_photo: Head-and-shoulders shot from a laptop webcam on a desk, angled slightly upwards so the top of the frame shows a bit of ceiling. Daylight from a window to his left lights one side of his face, and the other side is a little shadowed. He has a long, lean face with light stubber, pale skin slightly reddened at the cheeks, and short, neatly cut sandy-brown hair greying at the temples. He wears thin rectangular metal-framed glasses and a plain navy crew-neck jumper over a white collared shirt. His expression is neutral and attentive, mouth closed, eyebrows slightly raised as if waiting for a question. Behind him is a white-painted wall with a tall pale wooden bookcase holding several thick ring binders labelled with project codes, a few engineering reference books, a folded high-vis vest and a white hard hat on the top shelf. To the right of the frame the rear wheel of a black bicycle hangs on a wall hook. A small framed photo of a teenage girl on a beach sits on the edge of the shelf.
